title: The martyrs
hookLine: those tortured and killed who kept their faith and hair to the last breath

lines: AGAIN AND AGAIN, A CALM FACE.
cards: The Central Sikh Museum, inside the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar, has whole walls of paintings that are hard to look at.

Men and women in the middle of terrible suffering, and again and again, the same detail: their faces are calm. Children stop in front of them with their parents, and the parents explain, quietly, who each person was.
Those paintings illustrate, almost line by line, one passage of the Ardas: the one that remembers those who died rather than give up their faith.

teach.h: SINGHS AND SINGHNIS: MEN AND WOMEN.
teach.b: The passage begins: jinhaan singhaan singhneeaan ne, those Singhs and Singhnis, men and women both, who gave their heads for dharam, for faith and righteousness.
Then it names, briefly, what was done to them: cut apart joint by joint, scalped, broken on the wheel, sawn in two. Each phrase points to real people Sikhs remember by name.

Bhai Mati Das, sawn apart in Delhi at the time of Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom. Bhai Mani Singh, cut joint by joint at Lahore. Bhai Taru Singh, who tradition says chose to have his scalp removed rather than cut his hair.

teach.h: NAMED, PLAINLY, AND NOT LINGERED ON.
teach.b: It says what happened, plainly, and moves on. Then comes the line that gives today its carry: sikhee kesaan suaasaan naal nibaahee.

teach.h: KEPT SIKHI WITH THEIR HAIR, TO THE END.
teach.b: They kept Sikhi, with their kes, their uncut hair, to the last suaas, the last breath. Nibaahee is the verb from Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok about companions: kou na nibhio saath, no one saw it through.
Here the Ardas names the ones who did. And just before: dharam naheen haariaa. They did not lose their faith.
Not the fight; many of them lost that. They didn't lose the thing that mattered to them. That's how Sikhs remember martyrs, shaheed: not as victims, but as witnesses.
Shaheed is a word Punjabi shares with Arabic, where it carries the sense of a witness.
Why say this every day? Sikhs would say: so that no one forgets what was given for them, and so that the small daily choices of faith are held up beside the great ones.

how: In every Ardas Sikhs remember the men and women who gave their lives for their faith and kept Sikhi with their hair to the last breath, and gurdwaras and museums often display paintings of these martyrs.

games.q: the Ardas says of the martyrs: dharam naheen haariaa. what did they not lose?
games.why: many of them lost the fight and their lives. what they didn't lose was their faith, and that's how Sikhs remember them.

practice: Sit still and let your breath slow; you don't need to picture anything painful.

For a minute, just hold the fact that people gave everything for what they believed, and that their families still say their names, counting your breaths if it helps: suaas, breath. If you pray, end the silence with Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: The martyrs. Shaheed, the witnesses: Singhs and Singhnis who did not lose their faith, and kept Sikhi to the last breath.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: shaheed, martyr; from Arabic, a witness.

carryVoice: Your line: to the last breath. They saw it through, all the way. See you tomorrow.
